key_claim: A demand-responsive transit framework leveraging mobility-on-demand principles can optimize shared first- and last-mile connectivity in sparsely populated areas.
methodology: Novel design framework for shared first- and last-mile transit systems incorporating passenger commitment, trip consolidation, and service-level considerations, validated through a detailed case study.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address peer-to-peer or grassroots ridesharing coordination among specific user communities such as international students in small-town university settings.
theoretical_framework: Demand-responsive transit (DRT) / Mobility-on-Demand (MoD) service design framework

key_claim: University campuses serve as tractable testbeds for smart-system integration, but open challenges remain in sustainability, acceptability, ethics, and learning models.
methodology: Systematic literature review of 182 publications (2010–2020) categorized into seven smartness dimensions: smart building, environment, mobility, living, people, governance, and data.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address grassroots student-organized coordination platforms or identity-verified peer-to-peer mobility services on campuses.
theoretical_framework: Seven-category smart campus taxonomy (building, environment, mobility, living, people, governance, data)

key_claim: User perceptions of ride-hail services differ significantly from public bus perceptions along a high-trip-attraction corridor in Nagpur, India.
methodology: Combined online (Google form) and offline (bus stop intercept) survey along a 3.8 km corridor in Nagpur city, analyzing user perceptions of ride-hail versus public bus services.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address non-commercial peer-to-peer carpooling, identity verification, or safety trust mechanisms in ride-matching platforms.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey data from a 3.8 km corridor in Nagpur city
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: MaaS deployments improve accessibility, safety, energy efficiency, and employment while reducing congestion, but benefits depend heavily on spatial and temporal context.
methodology: Meta-analysis synthesizing 61 original articles from 2000 to 2022 quantitatively evaluating community benefits of MaaS deployments in rural and urban areas.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address grassroots, student-organized multi-module coordination platforms or identity-verified peer-to-peer carpooling in small-town university settings.
theoretical_framework: Mobility as a Service (MaaS) community-benefit evaluation framework

key_claim: User satisfaction with university-provided transit services is associated with specific demographic and service-quality factors identifiable through ordered logistic regression.
methodology: Descriptive statistics and ordered logistic regression applied to survey data from users of four public transit services at the University of Texas at Arlington.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address multi-module coordination across non-transit services (e.g., housing, social integration) for international students in small-town university settings.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of University of Texas at Arlington transit service users
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: A free women-only immunization carpool service in rural Pakistan is feasible and acceptable, with preliminary positive impact on childhood immunization coverage and timeliness.
methodology: Feasibility study across four immunization facilities in Shikarpur District, Sindh, using a branded carpool vehicle for women with un- or under-immunized children; demographic and service-experience data collected alongside immunization records from provincial electronic registry.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address peer-to-peer identity-verified carpooling or technology-mediated coordination; focuses on a centrally provided free transport service rather than grassroots or platform-mediated ride-sharing.
dataset_or_benchmark: Demographic and service-experience survey data from Shikarpur District
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Personal photos on Airbnb influence trust formation and reputation building in the sharing economy.
methodology: Not determinable from available metadata (abstract missing).
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address rating fairness from the perspective of service providers (e.g., drivers) or the role of identity verification beyond personal photos in multi-module coordination platforms.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Digital Reputation Systems used by platforms like Airbnb cannot be straightforwardly trusted because they embed power asymmetries that unfairly distribute benefits and burdens among companies, consumers, and workers.
methodology: Normative/ethical analysis of Digital Reputation Systems (DRSs) examining trust, reliability, and fairness of algorithmically constructed reputation scores across platform companies, consumers, and workers.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity-verified, community-specific platforms (e.g., university carpooling) where trust dynamics differ from large commercial platforms, nor empirical measurement of rating fairness across driver vs. rider subgroups.
theoretical_framework: Digital Reputation Systems (DRS) framework analyzing trust and power asymmetries in platform economies

key_claim: Distinguishing ticket-clipper and end-to-end professionalism models on e-hospitality platforms can contribute to sustainable sector growth in local and regional communities.
methodology: Hierarchical linear modeling using Airdna vacation rental data (HomeAway/Stayz) with a conceptual narrative distinguishing two professionalism dimensions.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity-verified peer coordination or safety mechanisms in non-hospitality sharing economy contexts such as carpooling.
theoretical_framework: Ticket-clipper vs. end-to-end professionalism model for sharing economy platforms

key_claim: Implicit rather than explicit host self-disclosure on Airbnb leads to higher guest trust, contrary to expectations.
methodology: Online experimental survey with two conditions (implicit vs. explicit self-disclosure) comparing 129 Dutch and 71 Chinese participants on booking intention and trust.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address trust formation in identity-verified platforms or non-accommodation sharing economy services like carpooling.
dataset_or_benchmark: Custom online experimental survey (N=200, 129 Dutch + 71 Chinese)
theoretical_framework: Self-disclosure theory applied cross-culturally to sharing economy trust

key_claim: Three types of online trust-building mechanisms differentially affect providers' trust in the sharing platform versus trust in consumers in peer-to-peer accommodation.
methodology: Structural equation modeling with partial least squares (PLS-SEM) on a sample of 209 providers on online short-term rental platforms (Airbnb, Xiaozhu).
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address trust from the consumer/rider perspective, nor trust mechanisms in mobility-sharing platforms or small-town university contexts.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 209 providers on Airbnb and Xiaozhu
theoretical_framework: Online trust-building mechanisms framework (institutional, interpersonal, and knowledge-based trust)

key_claim: Perceived risk heightened by COVID-19 negatively moderates the relationship between trust and usage intention for both Airbnb and Uber, with Airbnb exhibiting higher structural assurance and usage intentions.
methodology: Comparative quantitative study of Airbnb and Uber users examining trust antecedents (structural assurance, privacy protection, social influence) and COVID-19 risk moderation effects.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity-verified grassroots platforms, rating fairness for small driver pools, or trust dynamics in non-commercial peer carpooling contexts.
dataset_or_benchmark: Custom survey comparing Airbnb and Uber users
theoretical_framework: Trust transfer theory with perceived risk moderation in sharing economy services

key_claim: Customer-related, platform-related, and service-provider-related factors all significantly drive customer participation on sharing platforms, with customer motives and trust being key antecedents.
methodology: Meta-analysis of 192 independent samples from 167 studies involving 171,344 customers, synthesizing empirical findings on antecedents of customer participation on sharing platforms.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how identity-verification or safety design primitives within platforms moderate customer participation, nor grassroots coordination in small-town or university-specific contexts.
dataset_or_benchmark: Meta-analytic dataset of 167 studies / 192 independent samples / 171,344 customers
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Trust is the major determinant of purchase decisions in peer-to-peer accommodation platforms like Airbnb and Couchsurfing.
methodology: Umbrella-type literature review of secondary sources examining concepts, models, and theories applied by previous scholars to Airbnb and Couchsurfing.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity-verification mechanisms, rating fairness, or multi-module coordination challenges specific to non-accommodation sharing contexts such as carpooling.
dataset_or_benchmark: Secondary literature on Airbnb and Couchsurfing
theoretical_framework: Disruptive innovation model; network hospitality concept

key_claim: Same-race endorsements from previous white guests largely offset white guests' racial bias against non-white Airbnb hosts, making in-group bias in recommendations counteract rather than reinforce discrimination.
methodology: Observational analysis of Airbnb booking and review data examining in-group preference for same-race hosts and the moderating effect of same-race guest endorsements on host selection.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address whether identity-verification or platform design interventions (e.g., anonymization, gamification) could further reduce racial bias, nor whether findings generalize to non-accommodation sharing platforms like carpooling.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Corporate digital responsibility in the sharing economy can be conceptualized through three VBA categories—value, balance, and accountability—that capture tensions between platforms' responsibilities and irresponsibilities.
methodology: Conceptual extension of the value-balance-accountability (VBA) framework using an integrative perspective combining top-down and bottom-up approaches, with Airbnb and Uber as illustrative cases.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not empirically test the framework or address grassroots user-driven coordination, identity-verification design primitives, or rating-fairness mechanisms within platform governance.
dataset_or_benchmark: None (conceptual paper using Airbnb and Uber as illustrative cases)
theoretical_framework: Value-Balance-Accountability (VBA) framework

key_claim: Attitude significantly mediates the effects of effort expectancy, social influence, and facilitating conditions on Indian consumers' intention to use Airbnb.
methodology: Survey of 301 potential Indian consumers analyzed using an extended meta-UTAUT model with hedonic motivation, trust, and self-efficacy.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how identity verification or safety mechanisms affect trust and adoption in peer-to-peer sharing platforms.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 301 Indian potential Airbnb consumers
theoretical_framework: meta-UTAUT extended with hedonic motivation, trust, and self-efficacy

key_claim: Romanian tourists' motivations and digital skills significantly shape their acceptance and use of the Airbnb collaborative platform.
methodology: Cross-sectional quantitative survey with non-random convenience sampling of Romanian tourists to assess Airbnb awareness, motivations, and alignment with expectations.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address multi-module coordination challenges or grassroots self-organization among platform users in underserved settings.
dataset_or_benchmark: Convenience sample survey of Romanian tourists
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Specific trust-influencing factors mediate travelers' behavioral intention to use Airbnb across three ASEAN countries.
methodology: Mixed-methods approach combining self-administered questionnaires (N=130 Airbnb users from the Philippines, Indonesia, and Singapore) with informal interviews, analyzed using Hayes' Process Macro.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how platform-level identity verification or safety design primitives shape trust formation beyond self-reported perceptions.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 130 Airbnb users from the Philippines, Indonesia, and Singapore
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Consumer loyalty toward Airbnb is shaped by both dedication-based mechanisms (authentic experience, trust, social benefits) and constraint-based mechanisms (relative attractiveness, price fairness).
methodology: Structural equation modeling on survey data from 156 Airbnb consumers who used the platform more than twice, examining dedication-based and constraint-based commitment paths.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how rating fairness or gamification mechanisms influence loyalty in peer-to-peer platforms.
theoretical_framework: Dedication-based and constraint-based dual commitment framework for consumer loyalty

key_claim: Hybrid business models in the sharing economy integrate access, platform, and community-based economy elements, creating a balanced strategy that strengthens overall business operations.
methodology: Integrative literature review and synthesis of research on hybrid business models and the sharing economy, leading to a conceptual framework.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity verification, safety mechanisms, or grassroots coordination challenges faced by specific user subgroups such as international students in small-town settings.
theoretical_framework: Conceptual framework for Hybrid Business Models in the Sharing Economy encompassing value proposition, governance, coordination, resource allocation, sustainability, reputation, and communication channels

key_claim: Private chat groups on instant messaging apps afford food delivery workers communities of practice, resistance, and mutualism not provided by the delivery platforms themselves.
methodology: Multi-country qualitative study using participant observation in five countries (Italy, Spain, Mexico, China, India), in-depth interviews with 68 food delivery couriers, and digital ethnography within dozens of private online chat groups.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how self-organized digital coordination among platform workers translates into formalized multi-module platform design or identity-verified trust mechanisms.
dataset_or_benchmark: digital ethnography of private chat groups across five countries
theoretical_framework: Affordances-in-practice (Costa 2018) combined with communities of practice theory

key_claim: DonnaRosa, a WhatsApp-based community of practice among breast cancer specialists, effectively facilitates second-opinion exchange and professional networking through informal instant messaging.
methodology: Mixed-methods design: qualitative analysis of chat logs, an online survey of 54 members (92.5% response rate), and semi-structured interviews with founders and participants.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how informal professional communities of practice translate to non-specialist grassroots contexts or how identity verification and safety design primitives could strengthen such communities.
theoretical_framework: Community of Practice (CoP)

key_claim: Community WeChat groups significantly facilitate grassroots risk communication and interactive governance during pandemic crises in Shanghai megacity communities.
methodology: Online survey of 1006 residents across 350 communities in Shanghai with multiple linear regression analysis examining participant roles' impact on communication satisfaction and perceived quality.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how grassroots social media coordination extends beyond crisis communication to everyday multi-module coordination needs such as carpooling or resource sharing in non-megacity settings.
theoretical_framework: Community risk communication framework with interactive governance

key_claim: Self-organized spontaneous volunteers in Israel perceive their activity as effective and it strengthens their sense of belonging to community and state.
methodology: Case study using participant observation and semi-structured interviews with spontaneous self-organized volunteers in Israel during crisis situations.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how technology-enabled self-organized volunteering translates into sustained multi-module coordination platforms or how identity verification affects volunteer trust.
dataset_or_benchmark: Qualitative interviews and participant observation from Israeli volunteer crisis settings
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Residents' WeChat group use positively impacts pro-community behavior through serial mediation of community trust and community attachment.
methodology: Online survey of 500 commercial housing community residents in Wuhan, China, analyzed with structural equation modeling using SPSS 26.0 and Mplus 8.3.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address whether platform-mediated community coordination extends to multi-module service domains beyond crisis communication or to non-residential (e.g., campus) communities.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 500 Wuhan commercial housing community residents
theoretical_framework: Mediation model of community trust and community attachment linking WeChat group use to pro-community behavior

key_claim: Mobile instant messaging platforms like WhatsApp are used in boundary-crossing informal learning and knowledge sharing across diverse health professional groups in low-income countries.
methodology: Survey with open- and closed-ended questions administered to 40 respondents across 44 global health project settings, with mixed-methods analysis.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how MIM-based grassroots coordination could be formalized into verified, multi-module platforms or how safety and identity verification affect knowledge-sharing trust.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 40 respondents across 44 global health project settings
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: International students report higher fear of crime in the United States than in their home countries, and media consumption cultivates this fear.
methodology: Structural equation modeling (SEM) on a survey sample of 398 international students attending nine U.S. public and private universities.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how platform-based safety mechanisms such as identity verification or peer rating systems could mitigate international students' fear of crime in small-town university settings.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of 398 international students at 9 U.S. universities
theoretical_framework: Cultivation theory

key_claim: Social media significantly influences Chinese students' decisions to study in the United States through factors identified by the UTAUT model.
methodology: Model analysis approach using the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) framework to identify key factors influencing decision-making
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how Chinese students coordinate practical logistics (housing, transportation, daily needs) after arriving at U.S. campuses, especially in small-town settings.
theoretical_framework: Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT)

key_claim: Chinese parents of international students employ four distinct coping strategies to discuss depression with their children studying in the United States.
methodology: In-depth interviews with 13 Chinese parents of CISs analyzed using a constant comparative method
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how structural features of the university setting (e.g., small-town isolation, lack of coordinated support platforms) exacerbate or mitigate mental health challenges for Chinese international students.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Chinese overseas students in the U.S. during COVID-19 were pushed into immobility by simultaneous inability to return home and hostility in the host society, and deployed four sets of mobility repertoires to cope.
methodology: Qualitative case study using in-depth interviews with Chinese students in the United States during the COVID-19 pandemic
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how grassroots digital platforms or peer-coordinated systems (e.g., carpooling, mutual aid) helped students overcome practical mobility constraints in small-town university settings.
theoretical_framework: Immobility studies framework; mobility repertoires concept

key_claim: Hyper-locality combined with anonymity and ephemerality on Yik Yak shapes campus community identity in situated ways distinct from non-anonymous platforms.
methodology: Interview study of 18 Yik Yak users on a single urban American university campus
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how identity verification (as opposed to anonymity) in campus platforms affects trust, safety, and coordination quality for instrumental tasks like carpooling.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: GPS spoofing with location-based anonymous apps like Yik Yak enables passive surveying of college campus populations who express themselves candidly due to anonymity.
methodology: GPS hacking to collect geolocated posts from Yik Yak across multiple US college campuses; content and behavioral analysis of anonymous location-bounded feeds
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether campus-scoped anonymous content pools translate into actionable coordination or resource mobilization beyond self-expression
dataset_or_benchmark: Yik Yak posts collected via GPS spoofing across US college campuses
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Content analysis of 4,000 Yaks from 42 US campuses reveals the nature and distribution of discourse within campus-geofenced anonymous platforms.
methodology: Manual content analysis of 4,000 Yik Yak posts sampled from 42 US university campuses, categorized by content type and context
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether campus-bounded anonymous platforms can support identity-verified coordination or trust-building needed for safety-critical services like ridesharing
dataset_or_benchmark: 4,000 Yik Yak posts from 42 US university campuses
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Facebook resource-mobilization requests reveal how institutionally-seeded network ties enable social capital dynamics through broadcasted favor and help requests.
methodology: Analysis of Facebook status update resource requests (questions, information requests, favors) and their responses to study social capital mobilization
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether resource mobilization via general-purpose social networks can extend to safety-critical multi-module coordination tasks such as carpooling among international students
theoretical_framework: social capital theory

key_claim: Facebook use among college students with .edu-gated identity verification is positively associated with bridging, bonding, and maintained social capital.
methodology: Survey of Michigan State University undergraduates measuring Facebook use intensity and its relationship to three forms of social capital
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether .edu-scoped identity gating translates into trust sufficient for offline safety-critical coordination such as ridesharing rather than just online social capital accumulation
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey of Michigan State University undergraduates
theoretical_framework: social capital theory (bridging, bonding, maintained social capital)

key_claim: Location-based filtering on Yik Yak manufactures a bounded campus identity even without explicit .edu credential verification.
methodology: Qualitative exploration of Yik Yak using the SIDE (social identity model of deindividuation effects) framework
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether location-manufactured identity is sufficient for trust in high-stakes coordination tasks like ridesharing versus low-stakes anonymous posting
theoretical_framework: SIDE (Social Identity Model of Deindividuation Effects)

key_claim: A single-click Android SOS app transmitting real-time GPS location via SMS to pre-registered contacts enhances women's personal security in emergencies.
methodology: Design and development of an Android safety application with real-time location tracking, emergency alerts, fake call system, and SOS; effectiveness evaluated via user feedback
what_it_does_NOT_address: Identity verification of helpers or coordination among multiple safety contacts to prevent false alarms or misuse
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Combining real-time GPS tracking, crime heatmap visualization, Dijkstra-based safe routing with crime weightage, and an AI chatbot in a web application provides comprehensive women's safety support.
methodology: Web application development using React.js, Node.js, Firebase, Socket.IO, Google Gemini API; features include GPS tracking, audio recording, crime heatmaps, Dijkstra safe routing, license plate verification, and AI chatbot
what_it_does_NOT_address: User identity verification, trust calibration among users, or empirical evaluation of safety outcomes with real users
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: SOS apps are shifting from manual panic-button models to context-aware, sensor-fused, AI-assisted systems integrated with police or monitoring networks, yet significant technological gaps remain.
methodology: Systematic review of eight major SOS and personal-safety apps synthesizing 20+ peer-reviewed studies, industry reports, and government evaluations (2020–2025)
what_it_does_NOT_address: Multi-module coordination platforms combining safety with other campus services, or identity-verified peer-to-peer trust mechanisms beyond authority-alerting
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Existing ride-sharing platforms lack continuous group-level situational awareness and safety-oriented coordination for real-time group travel.
methodology: Literature review of real-time location tracking, WebSocket-based communication, distance monitoring algorithms, and privacy-aware group mobility systems
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity verification or trust mechanisms for rider–driver matching in small-town or university contexts
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Games and gamification can simultaneously impact multiple climate change engagement dimensions including behavioral change and education.
methodology: Systematic literature review of 64 research outputs comprising 56 different gamified approaches for climate change engagement
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address gamification applied to peer-to-peer mobility coordination or carpooling platforms in university settings
dataset_or_benchmark: Corpus of 64 research outputs on gamified climate change engagement
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Gamification promotes environmentally responsible behavior in Ant Forest's postadoption stage through psychological need satisfaction and belief/attitude persuasion.
methodology: Survey-based empirical study (N=1869) with a model grounded in persuasion and motivation theories and the affordances–psychological outcomes–behavioral outcomes framework
limitation: Research community has primarily focused on adoption and continuation intention, paying limited attention to postadoption environmentally responsible behavior
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address gamification for coordination behaviors such as carpooling or multi-module platform engagement in small-town university contexts
dataset_or_benchmark: 1869 survey responses regarding Ant Forest usage
theoretical_framework: Affordances–psychological outcomes–behavioral outcomes framework combined with persuasion and motivation theories

key_claim: The convergence of machine learning and gamification is primarily applied in learning, personalization, behavioral change, context adaptation, and data collection.
methodology: Systematic literature review investigating the intersection of gamification and machine learning technologies
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how ML-gamification convergence could enhance rating fairness or driver supply incentives in identity-verified peer-to-peer platforms
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Gamified challenges based on walking distances and intra-team goals significantly enhanced engagement and improved sustainable mobility behaviors among high school participants.
methodology: 13-week school-based intervention using GPS-tracked commuting data and self-report surveys via the Play&Go gamified app, analyzing challenge types, HEXAD player types, and Big Five traits.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether gamified mobility interventions generalize beyond high school students to other populations such as university or international student communities.
dataset_or_benchmark: High School Challenge 2024 campaign data (Lecco, Italy)
theoretical_framework: HEXAD Player Types and Big Five personality traits

key_claim: Eco Drive integrates GPS tracking, user input, and gamification to empower individuals to reduce travel-related carbon emissions through sustainable travel choices.
methodology: Design and implementation of a Java-based mobile application combining GPS tracking, user input, and gamification features for carbon footprint tracking.
what_it_does_NOT_address: How identity verification, safety, or coordination across multiple mobility modules (e.g., carpooling matching) can be supported within such a platform.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Factors from the Technology Acceptance Model significantly predict primary school pupils' adoption of the ClassCraft gamification platform for sustainable mobility education.
methodology: Mixed-methods study combining a Focus Group with 6 students and a TAM-based questionnaire with 75 pupils aged 10–11 using the ClassCraft gamified platform.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether gamification-based sustainable mobility education translates into actual long-term behavioral change in transport mode choices.
dataset_or_benchmark: Questionnaire data from 75 primary school pupils
theoretical_framework: Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)

key_claim: VR gaming environments enable citizens to experience and provide feedback on smart city applications, creating a significant feedback loop for urban planning.
methodology: Development of a VR gaming environment for a real-world future city project in Istanbul, allowing users to explore smart city applications via four circulation modes.
what_it_does_NOT_address: How grassroots coordination needs of specific user populations (e.g., international students) can be integrated into gamified urban planning platforms.
dataset_or_benchmark: Real-world future city project for 50,000 inhabitants in Istanbul, Turkey
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Trust-building mechanisms in P2P carpooling platforms have different effects for car owners vs. non-owners and for experienced vs. inexperienced users.
methodology: Mixed-method: qualitative comparison of trust-building mechanisms across four carpooling platforms plus a laboratory experiment (N=163)
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity-verification as a trust-building primitive or trust dynamics specific to international/minority student populations in small-town contexts.
theoretical_framework: Distinguishes online trust, implicit trust, and reason-based trust as conceptual categories

key_claim: Algorithm-based telematics scoring can improve trust-building in P2P carsharing over traditional peer ratings by addressing fake and biased rating problems.
methodology: Design case study: 16 problem-centered interviews, co-design of an app with scored profiles, and evaluation with 12 participants
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address fairness asymmetries between driver and rider subgroups in rating systems or gamification as a trust/engagement mechanism.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Hiding feedback until both parties submit reviews (simultaneous unveiling) reduces reciprocity bias in two-sided reputation systems.
methodology: Large-scale field experiment on Airbnb manipulating the timing of feedback revelation (simultaneous vs. sequential unveiling)
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address rating fairness asymmetries between active drivers and passive riders in carpooling contexts, nor identity-verified community platforms.
theoretical_framework: Two-sided reputation system design with reciprocity and unveiling mechanisms

key_claim: CHI 2014 paper sample sizes range from 1 to 916,000 with a modal value of N=12, varying systematically by study type.
methodology: Systematic analysis of all CHI 2014 papers cataloging sample sizes and study types
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address whether small-sample findings in formative HCI studies generalize to deployment-scale platforms or how subgroup analyses (e.g., driver vs. rider) should be powered.
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Evolutionary game theory shows platform promotion policies can counteract rating-based discrimination against marginalised groups while maintaining service quality incentives.
methodology: Evolutionary game theoretical model analyzing platform promotion strategies under biased reputation systems
what_it_does_NOT_address: Empirical validation with real platform data or user studies; does not address multi-module coordination in small-town university contexts or identity-verified carpooling scenarios.
theoretical_framework: Evolutionary game theory applied to platform reputation systems

key_claim: Algorithmic management creates a gray zone blurring employee-freelancer boundaries, posing unique challenges that conventional HRM and organizational behavior frameworks fail to address.
methodology: Comprehensive literature review synthesizing HRM, organizational psychology, and organizational behavior research on algorithmic management
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address grassroots self-organized coordination by users (e.g., international students) as a response to algorithmic management gaps, nor small-town or university-specific platform contexts.
theoretical_framework: Gray zone conceptual framework for algorithmic management spanning HRM, OP, and OB

key_claim: Combining mutual escrow, bidirectional dynamic rating, and a cooldown period on blockchain reduces rating manipulation and retaliatory feedback in decentralized ridesharing.
methodology: Blockchain-based system design incorporating mutual escrow, bidirectional dynamic rating with historical consistency adjustment, and a cooldown period for rating submissions
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity verification as a trust mechanism, gamification incentives for driver supply, or the specific rating fairness dynamics observed in small driver-subgroup populations.
theoretical_framework: Blockchain-based mutual escrow and dynamic reputation framework

key_claim: Synthesizing 58 interdisciplinary studies reveals pervasive discrimination in digital sharing economy platforms is enabled by specific design decisions that can be mitigated through targeted software design strategies.
methodology: Systematic literature review of 58 interdisciplinary studies identifying discrimination concerns, triggering features, and mitigation strategies in DSE platforms
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address university-specific or small-town contexts, identity-verified multi-module platforms, or how grassroots user coordination fills gaps left by platform design.
theoretical_framework: Software design perspective on anti-discrimination strategies in digital sharing economy

key_claim: Algorithmic management practices negatively influence workplace well-being both directly and indirectly through reduced job autonomy and altered total rewards perceptions.
methodology: Conceptual model tested empirically using survey data from European organisations, analysing relationships between algorithmic management, job autonomy, total rewards and workplace well-being.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not examine algorithmic management in grassroots or peer-to-peer platforms where users voluntarily coordinate, nor small-scale community-driven contexts outside formal employer–employee relationships.
theoretical_framework: Conceptual model linking algorithmic management practices, job autonomy, total rewards and workplace well-being

key_claim: Nurse-facilitated WeChat patient groups function as closed clinic-scoped coordination infrastructure supporting patient care within bounded communities.
methodology: Qualitative study of nurse-facilitated patient groups on WeChat examining how a super-app is repurposed as bounded community coordination infrastructure in Chinese clinical settings.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not examine how closed-community coordination on super-apps generalises to non-healthcare contexts such as student-organised multi-module platforms in small-town university settings.
dataset_or_benchmark: WeChat patient group interaction data from Chinese clinics
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: LINE exemplifies super-app platformization in East Asia, evolving from single-purpose chat to an integrated do-everything platform reshaping cultural production.
methodology: Platform studies analysis of LINE as a super app, examining platformization processes and their transformative effects on cultural production in East Asia.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how super-app integrated design principles translate to grassroots, identity-verified community platforms or student-driven multi-module coordination in resource-constrained settings.
theoretical_framework: Platformization / platform studies framework applied to East Asian super-app ecosystems

key_claim: Japanese families use LINE as bounded intergenerational social infrastructure, with matriarchal connections playing a central role in maintaining familial ties via the platform.
methodology: Ethnographic fieldwork with 12 Japanese families over 3 years examining intergenerational use of LINE as social mobile media.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not examine whether bounded-scope family coordination on an integrated platform generalises to non-kin communities such as international student groups or multi-module campus platforms.
dataset_or_benchmark: Ethnographic data from 12 Japanese families over 3 years
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: KakaoTalk chatrooms function as dwelling places structured into primary, secondary, and tertiary closed functional regions for social interaction.
methodology: Ethnographic study of KakaoTalk chatroom usage patterns
what_it_does_NOT_address: How closed-community coordination in messaging apps translates to multi-module service coordination for newcomer populations such as international students
theoretical_framework: Dwelling places framework (primary/secondary/tertiary functional regions)

key_claim: Integrating Mobility-as-a-Feature with the 15-minute city concept into local super apps can drive equitable and sustainable urban transitions.
methodology: Perspective/conceptual paper combining literature review, practical application examples, and a user survey (N=1,019)
what_it_does_NOT_address: Whether local super apps are viable in small-town or university settings lacking dense urban infrastructure, and how identity verification and safety mechanisms factor into such platforms
theoretical_framework: Mobility-as-a-Feature (MaaF) integrated with the 15-minute city (15mC) concept

key_claim: Public perception of PUSAKA Super Apps digitizing Ministry of Religious Affairs services is generally positive but hampered by server and network errors.
methodology: Quantitative survey of PUSAKA users collecting perceptions of digitized government services
limitation: Server and network errors remain obstacles to effective service delivery
what_it_does_NOT_address: How government super-app adoption dynamics differ from grassroots community-driven multi-module platforms addressing coordination gaps in small-town or university contexts
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: SANTER's development as a super-app for Samarinda's smart city transformation faces knowledge, practical, and population gaps requiring a strategic roadmap for inclusive evolution.
methodology: Qualitative descriptive approach using in-depth stakeholder interviews, observations, and document analysis
what_it_does_NOT_address: How grassroots user self-organization and peer-to-peer coordination mechanisms (e.g., carpooling, safety, gamification) operate outside top-down government-driven super-app initiatives
dataset_or_benchmark: Stakeholder interviews with city officials, SANTER administrators, and citizens; document analysis
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: Herzberg's and Taylor's motivation theories explain contingent gig worker motivation in China's mobile food delivery aggregator platforms Meituan and Ele.me.
methodology: Qualitative study drawing on Herzberg and Taylor motivation theories with thematic analysis of gig workers at Chinese MFDAs
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address peer-to-peer coordination or safety mechanisms among gig workers outside employer-controlled platforms
dataset_or_benchmark: Qualitative data from Meituan and Ele.me gig workers in China
theoretical_framework: Herzberg two-factor theory and Taylor scientific management theory

key_claim: Higher education and longer work experience among gig workers are associated with heightened concerns about algorithmic fairness, job stability, and support mechanisms.
methodology: Survey of 102 gig workers in Chennai analyzed with non-parametric tests (Kruskal-Wallis and Chi-square) across five perception dimensions
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address identity verification, grassroots self-organization, or multi-module coordination among gig workers outside commercial platforms
dataset_or_benchmark: Primary survey data from 102 gig workers in Chennai
theoretical_framework: none

key_claim: The temporariness of Working Holiday Visas fosters distinct worker subjectivities that make precarious platform work acceptable for highly educated young migrants.
methodology: Biographical qualitative exploration tracing migration trajectories of Chilean and Argentinian WHV gig workers in Germany using a temporalities lens
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how migrant gig workers self-organize grassroots coordination tools or identity-verified peer platforms to mitigate precarity
dataset_or_benchmark: Biographical interviews with Chilean and Argentinian WHV gig workers in Germany
theoretical_framework: Temporalities and becoming framework applied to migration and visa regimes

key_claim: Uganda's existing employment, social protection, and taxation laws are structurally inadequate to regulate platform-mediated gig work due to worker classification contradictions and enforcement limitations.
methodology: Critical legal review using labour law theory, platform governance theory, and regulatory compliance frameworks with case studies from ride-hailing, freelancing, and delivery platforms
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address grassroots worker-driven platform alternatives or community-based coordination mechanisms that could complement regulatory approaches
dataset_or_benchmark: Case studies from Ugandan ride-hailing, digital freelancing, and delivery platforms
theoretical_framework: Labour law theory, platform governance theory, and regulatory compliance frameworks

key_claim: Occupational context structures freelancers' capacity to interpret and navigate platform management, producing distinct experiences across self-presentation, flexibility, skilling, and sustainability.
methodology: Longitudinal qualitative analysis of 108 online freelancers across five occupational categories on digital labor platforms.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how identity-verified multi-module platforms could tailor coordination support to different occupational subgroups within a shared campus ecosystem.
dataset_or_benchmark: Longitudinal dataset of 108 online freelancers across five occupational categories
theoretical_framework: Occupational embeddedness framework for platform labor (platformic management × occupational context interaction)

key_claim: Job autonomy exerts a dual (positive and negative) influence on gig workers' workplace well-being through cognitive-affective mediating pathways.
methodology: Moderated dual-mediator model grounded in the cognitive-affective processing system (CAPS) framework, tested via survey of gig workers in China.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how platform design primitives such as identity verification, gamification, or rating fairness could modulate the autonomy–well-being relationship.
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey data from gig workers in China
theoretical_framework: Cognitive-Affective Processing System (CAPS) framework

key_claim: Food-delivery gig workers engage in sensemaking to cope with technical opacity and power asymmetry created by algorithmic management that replaces human managers.
methodology: Qualitative study of food-delivery platform workers examining sensemaking processes under algorithmic management.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address whether grassroots peer-coordination mechanisms or identity-verified community platforms could reduce the opacity and power asymmetry workers experience.
theoretical_framework: Sensemaking theory applied to algorithmic management

key_claim: Amazon fulfillment center workers develop nuanced resistance practices against labor-tracking algorithmic systems, extending CSCW's understanding of algorithmic management beyond gig work.
methodology: Two-year ethnographic study of Amazon fulfillment center workers examining reactions to productivity rates, managerial interventions, and quantified objectification.
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address algorithmic management in voluntary peer-to-peer coordination platforms or how design primitives like gamification and rating fairness apply to non-employer-controlled settings.
dataset_or_benchmark: Ethnographic data from Amazon fulfillment centers
theoretical_framework: Labor process theory (work games / resistance to algorithmic control)

key_claim: Gig economy has its own inherent logic as a stage in the evolution of employee-employer relations but has significantly reduced work quality.
methodology: Systematic literature review and analysis of current world literature on gig economy driving forces and development prospects
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address grassroots coordination mechanisms that gig workers or platform users self-organize outside formal platform structures
theoretical_framework: Multi-stage evolutionary framework of employee-employer relations from industrial to digital platform-mediated work

key_claim: Algorithmic control shapes gig workers' engagement through psychological contracts, with standardized guidance enhancing and tracking/constraints diminishing relational contracts.
methodology: Three-wave survey of 328 gig workers in China examining algorithmic control dimensions, psychological contracts, and work engagement with moderation by perceived algorithmic fairness
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how peer-to-peer or community-organized platforms without centralized algorithmic control affect worker engagement and fairness perceptions
dataset_or_benchmark: Three-wave survey of 328 Chinese gig workers
theoretical_framework: Psychological contract theory combined with perceived algorithmic fairness as moderator

key_claim: Different dimensions of algorithmic control have divergent effects on food delivery riders' mental health and risky riding behavior mediated by work pressure.
methodology: Survey of 466 Chinese food delivery riders analyzed using structural equation modeling and bootstrap methods, with work pressure as mediator and perceived autonomy as moderator
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how identity-verified community-based platforms might mitigate the psychological harms of algorithmic control on gig workers
dataset_or_benchmark: Survey data from 466 Chinese food delivery riders
theoretical_framework: Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model

key_claim: Four algorithmic control mechanisms — GPS tracking, rating systems, dynamic pricing, and automated sanctions — create distinct psychological risk pathways for public transport drivers.
methodology: PRISMA-guided systematic integrative review of 48 peer-reviewed studies (2016–2025) from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed with thematic synthesis
what_it_does_NOT_address: Does not address how user-governed or community-organized transport platforms with identity verification and gamification might alter these psychological risk pathways
dataset_or_benchmark: 48 peer-reviewed studies from Scopus, Web of Science, and PubMed (2016–2025)
theoretical_framework: Integrated multilevel framework synthesizing Job Demand-Control Model, Conservation of Resources Theory, and Algorithmic Management Theory
